The intended sound is not neighing (al-sahil), but rather their saying "ah, ah" (ḥ ḥ), as Ibn 'Abbas said. The word "ḍabḥan" is in the accusative either by its omitted verb, or by "al-'adiyat" because it conveys its meaning, or as a circumstantial accusative (al-ḥāliyya).

﴿And striking sparks of fire﴾ means: they strike fire with their hooves. Al-qadaḥ is the striking used to produce fire, and al-iyrā' (striking sparks) follows from it, since it is the bringing out and kindling of fire. So its "sparking" is what is seen from their hooves striking the stones, and it is called the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib. Since it is consequent upon their running, it is joined to it with "fa" (then). The Imam said: This is a description that befalls the horses from the purpose for which they were made to run, namely that they run and their running intensifies until sparks fly from their hooves, so that they may fall upon the enemy at dawn, which is the time of surprise, when the enemy is caught unprepared.

So it is permitted that this be intended here, meaning the shouting of those who fall upon the enemy and strike them, not the shouting of the raider against the fighter, although that is permissible with some remoteness. There are other possibilities in it, such as its referring to the running or to the raid, since it is interpreted as running. Then the bāʾ is causal or of association. It may also be adverbial. Likewise is depiction by the present tense after the past.

And they have let noble horses abandon their lands for other lands.

Then he said: God swears by horses possessed of those qualities whose mention He raised, in order to confirm the report that came in His words:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[6–8] ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ ﴿And indeed, he is a witness to that﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 7] ﴿And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8]

﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful﴾: that is, ungrateful (kafur), who denies His blessings and does not give thanks for them, meaning he does not use them in what is fitting, so as to reach Him through them.

Al-Mahayimi said: That is, indeed he is ungrateful, so this requires that He destroy him with these horses and subdue him with this anger. And from Abu Umamah: The kanud (ungrateful one) is the one who eats alone, beats his servant, and withholds his gift.

﴿And indeed, he is a witness to that﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 7]: that is, indeed mankind, in his ingratitude, is a witness who testifies against himself by it, because the effect of it is manifest upon him. So "witness" is used metaphorically for the manifestation of the traces of his disbelief and disobedience through the tongue of his state.

Al-Qashani said: By the testimony of his intellect and the light of his innate nature, that he does not fulfil the rights of Allah's blessings, and falls short towards Allah by his ingratitude.

﴿And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 8]: that is, indeed he is strong in his love of wealth and in preferring it over the world, while his love for fearing Allah and giving thanks for His blessing is weak and sluggish; and indeed, his love of the good that leads to the truth is intense, contracted and not open and expansive. Or the lam is for causation, meaning: indeed, because of his love of wealth he is miserly, and therefore he hides behind it, sinking his head into acquiring, preserving, gathering and withholding it, preoccupied with it away from the truth, turning away from its side.

The discussion on the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His saying, exalted is He:

[9–11] ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered forth,﴾ ﴿and what is in the breasts is obtained?﴾ (al-'Adiyat: 10) ﴿Indeed, their Lord, that Day, is fully Acquainted with them.﴾ (al-'Adiyat: 11)

﴿Does he not know﴾, meaning: after this veiling (heedlessness) and opposition to reason, does he not know by the light of his innate nature and the strength of his intellect ﴿when what is in the graves is scattered forth﴾, meaning: when what is in the graves is raised up and stirred out, and its dead are brought forth.

﴿And what is in the breasts is obtained﴾ (al-'Adiyat: 10), meaning: what is most manifest and apparent of the secrets, intentions, and hidden purposes within their breasts and souls, whether good or evil.

﴿Indeed, their Lord, that Day, is fully Acquainted with them﴾ (al-'Adiyat: 11), meaning: He is Knowing of their secrets, their inner thoughts, and their deeds, so He will recompense them according to them on that Day. The placing of the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) first is either for the sake of the arrangement of rhymed prose (*saj'*) and observing the verse-endings (*fawasil*), or for specification, since the occurrence of His knowledge is a metonymy for His recompense, and recompense only takes place on that Day.

Al-Razi said: The reason He singled out the deeds of the hearts for "obtaining" rather than the deeds of the limbs is that the deeds of the limbs follow the deeds of the hearts. For were it not for the motives and intentions in the hearts, the actions of the limbs would not come about. For this reason, He made the hearts the root in blame, saying ﴿his heart is sinful﴾ (al-Baqarah: 283), and the root in praise, saying ﴿their hearts tremble﴾ (al-Anfal: 2).
